title: Plum and the Frosting Fountain
markdown:
The sun burst through Hattie’s window, gold zigzags on the floor. Dawn. Today was the Grand Annual Bakery Fair. She bounced out of bed, feet a blur, brain buzzing like a happy bumblebee: sugary creations, dazzling decorations. Most of all she could not wait for Plum, the quiet gentle bakery unicorn. Plum was usually as silent as a secret on a breeze, but she had brilliant sparkly ideas. She just needed a nudge into the chaos. “Best brain waves,” Hattie told the door, “sometimes stuck in a cloud of vanilla-scented thoughts.”

Downstairs, sneakers squeaking. Warm bread and sugary cookies already filled the air. Dad, apron floured, nodded. “Ready for the big day?”

“Born ready.” She snagged a plump blueberry muffin, still warm. “Where’s Plum? I need her now.”

Plum was in her favourite quiet corner, coat the colour of spun sugar, dusting delicate cookies with shimmering pink sparkle. Silvery mane like a moonlit waterfall. Horn a pearly spiral, vanilla-scented glow that always calmed Hattie’s loudest bursts. She looked like a perfectly frosted cupcake waiting.

“Plum. The fair is today. You have to help with the frosting fountain. Spectacular. Breathtakingly, magnificently spectacular.”

Plum blinked liquid brown eyes. “The fair is always so busy. Noise. People bumping. I prefer dusting cookies. Quiet work.” A little sigh that smelled of vanilla.

“Cascades of bright pink, blueberry blue, lemon yellow, swirling like a delicious rainbow. People will gasp. They’ll cheer. Your magical touch. Your quiet thinking. We need both.”

Plum twitched a sparkly ear. “My quiet thinking often gets lost when there’s too much bouncing. And spluttering.” She looked at Hattie’s knees, which were already practising.

“We’ll be the best team. You do the quiet thinking. I’ll do the enthusiastic doing.” Hattie giggled and took Plum’s velvety muzzle. “Brilliant. No sudden sprints. I’ll try not to knock anything over.”

Plum’s second sigh held vanilla and hesitant agreement. “Alright. No sudden sprints.”

They hurried to the main town square, where the fair was already buzzing. Booths popped up like colourful mushrooms after rain. Bright banners snapped in the brisk morning air, fluttering like excited flags. A child ran past with a cookie almost as big as a hat. And there it was: the magnificent frosting fountain, tall and tiered, a gleaming silver marvel built by the town’s cleverest inventor. Today it was supposed to pour glorious rivers of shimmering delicious frosting for everyone to taste.

But as they arrived, a terrible sound sputtered from it. Gurgle. Hiss. Splutter. No frosting. Not a single solitary drop. A small crowd of worried bakers, faces etched, had gathered around. “Oh dear,” Hattie whispered. “That sounds bad.”

“Oh no.” Her earlier excitement drained like water from a leaky cup. “It’s broken. The fair starts in thirty minutes. Thirty minutes.” She peered into the fountain’s intricate workings, brow furrowed. “Is it the gears? The pipes? Maybe the frosting-goo pump has gotten clogged?” She poked and prodded, fingers covered in sticky unsprayed frosting base that smelled faintly of sugar and disappointment. “It’s just stuck. Completely stuck.” A familiar fizz of panic. This was not good.

She grabbed a small shiny wrench. “Maybe if I twist this really hard.” A jarring clang. A prominent bolt turned.

Plum watched, large gentle eyes thoughtful. She did not dart or poke. She looked. Head tilted, listening to the fountain’s sad sighs. She sniffed; the vanilla from her horn deepened. Hattie was too busy with the wrench to notice the thinking face.

“Hattie. Stop. Don’t twist that. It is not a twisty problem.”

Hattie paused, wrench still in hand. “Then what? Quickly. We haven’t a moment.”

Plum stepped closer, hooves silent on cobbles. “It’s quiet. The motor is trying. I can hear it. It has forgotten how to push. Shy. It needs encouragement. Not force.”

“A shy motor?” Hattie blinked. Peculiar. Bonkers, even.

“A gentle nudge. A reminder.” Plum lowered her head and nudged a tiny almost-invisible lever near the base with the tip of her horn, tucked behind a decorative swirl of metal. A click, almost too quiet.

Suddenly, with a joyful rush and a happy contented hum, the frosting fountain sprang to life. Rivers of pink, blue, and yellow frosting cascaded down the tiers, smelling like pure happiness and sun-ripened summer berries. The crowd of bakers erupted in cheers, worries melting away like sugar in warm milk. Hattie threw her arms around Plum in a big enthusiastic hug. “You fixed it. How did you know? It was so clever.”

Plum’s slow warm smile. “Sometimes the quietest things have the biggest answers. You were trying to force it. It needed a reminder of its purpose.”

The bakery fair was a spectacular success. Laughter bounced and echoed through the square like happy fireflies. The frosting fountain was the undeniable star, everyone dipping cookies, cakes, and even fingers into the delightful streams. A baker offered Plum a sugar-cookie thank-you; she dusted it once more, out of habit. Hattie, bursting with pride, kept Plum close, occasionally sharing a knowing glance about their odd partnership. Plum, still quiet and gentle, beamed with every happy splash, unicorn magic proving itself in the most delicious way. Boundless energy and quiet wisdom: a perfect recipe. They did not skip off to decorate a million cookies. They stood in the spray-scent and let the fountain do the spectacular part, which, it turned out, had only ever needed a hidden lever and a unicorn who listened before she twisted.
